chunks: Inductor current in PFM mode. The question: What happens to the inductor current?
In PFM the inductor current is not one continuous up-and-down wave. It is a train of separate triangle-shaped pulses, with the current at zero between them.
Each pulse has the same peak. What changes with the load is how often the pulses appear.
Picture a skyline of identical triangular mountains with flat plains between them. Each mountain is one pulse: the current climbs steadily, then falls steadily back to the ground.
At light load the plains are wide. As the load rises, the plains shrink until the mountains stand side by side.
The analogy fits the shape, but remember the flat parts are real: the inductor truly carries no current there.
The pulse is an asymmetric triangle: a steep rise (1. 85 amps/µs) while the high side is on and a gentler fall (0.
70 amps/µs) while the low side conducts, because V in-V out is 2. 6 times V out . The area is 0. 354 µC, the charge delivered to the output and load per pulse.
The 20 milliamps load line is barely visible at the bottom, which shows how far the peak sticks out above the average.
Peak current: the fixed height each pulse climbs to before turning around.
Slope: how fast the current changes: (V in-V out) over L going up, V out over L going down ("What sets the inductor current slope").
Zero-current detector: a circuit that turns the bottom switch off when the current reaches zero.
Saturation current: the current above which the inductor suddenly loses most of its inductance, so the current shoots up. Burst: a group of pulses fired together.
Take 12 volts in, 3. 3 volts out and a 4. 7 microhenries inductor, with a 0. 6 amps peak. Going up, the slope is 8. 7 over 4. 7 micro about 1.
85 amps/µs, so the climb takes about 0. 32 microseconds. Going down, the slope is 3. 3 over 4. 7 micro about 0. 70 amps/µs, so the fall takes about 0. 86 microseconds.
The whole triangle lasts about 1. 2 microseconds, and then the current stays at zero until the output sags. That is the whole idea.
"In PFM the inductor current is a train of triangular pulses with zero current in between.
Each pulse ramps up at (V in-V out) over L to a fixed peak, ramps back down at V out over L to zero, where the low side shuts off.
Then the inductor sits idle while the capacitor feeds the load. The pulse shape doesn't change with load, only how often they occur.
Peak current is much higher than the average, and near half the peak they run back to back and the converter hands over to PWM."
